title: OpenAI Jalapeno Custom AI ASIC at Hot Chips 2026
gist: OpenAI, with Broadcom, took its in-house Jalapeno inference ASIC from architecture concept to running ChatGPT in about 15 months, and at 700W it beats Nvidia's 1.2-1.4kW GB200/GB300 on throughput-per-kilowatt and latency across GPT-OSS, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K2.5 (e.g. 1.9x throughput/kW and 1.7x lower latency vs GB200 on GPT-OSS-120B) even while using simpler single-token prediction against Nvidia's multi-token baselines; OpenAI used its own internal AI model plus the XLS hardware description language to speed chip design (56% PPA win on a BF16 multiply unit vs. a human baseline) and built a spatial, AI-friendly programming model (Gluon) explicitly so that AI systems, not just humans, can efficiently map, place, and schedule workloads on the hardware.

themes.theme: Speed and structure of OpenAI's silicon program

insights.claim: OpenAI took Jalapeno from architecture concept (late 2024) through RTL freeze (2025), tapeout (late 2025), Codex running on the chip (early 2026), to ChatGPT running on it shortly after — a full custom ASIC design cycle in roughly nine months from initial RTL to tapeout, and about 15 months end-to-end from concept to production use.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A ~9-month RTL-to-tapeout cycle is dramatically faster than typical 2-3 year custom silicon programs; if OpenAI's AI-assisted design methodology is generalizable, it implies other well-capitalized AI labs/hyperscalers could compress their own custom-silicon timelines, accelerating the broader shift away from merchant GPUs faster than previously assumed.
insights.quote: This project moved quickly once OpenAI concluded that inference and agentic workloads needed a purpose-built design.

insights.claim: Jalapeno is explicitly framed by OpenAI as an inference platform (ASIC plus host and accelerator rack) rather than a raw standalone accelerator chip, targeting state-of-the-art performance-per-watt at low latency for multi-chip workloads.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Framing the product as a full inference platform (not just a chip) signals OpenAI intends to control the entire system stack for its own internal inference economics, reducing dependence on Nvidia's complete rack-level offerings (GB200 NVL72, etc.) for its highest-volume production workload.
insights.quote: OpenAI Jalapeño is framed as an inference platform rather than a raw accelerator.
insights.locator: OpenAI Jalapeno ASIC at Hot Chips 2026

themes.theme: Benchmark methodology: latency and energy, not raw specs

insights.claim: OpenAI deliberately frames its comparisons around two metrics — time to last token (user experience) and tokens per joule (inference efficiency) — plotting systems along the full Pareto frontier of latency versus energy per token, rather than chasing raw chip counts, throughput per chip, or time to first token.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a meaningful reframing of how AI inference hardware should be evaluated — investors and buyers benchmarking accelerators should adopt latency-vs-energy-per-token as the relevant unit economics lens rather than peak FLOPS, since it better reflects real production inference cost and user experience tradeoffs.
insights.quote: OpenAI frames the design around two metrics, time to last token for user experience and tokens per joule for inference efficiency.
insights.locator: Metrics that matter: latency and energy

insights.claim: OpenAI uses InferenceX, a public power-normalized benchmark spanning the full prefill-to-decode spectrum across a basket of open-source models, normalizing to package TDP: Jalapeno at 700W versus GB200 at 1.2kW and GB300/MI355X at 1.4kW, measured against the July 2026 Pareto frontier.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Jalapeno's headline power disadvantage (700W) versus GB200/GB300 (1.2-1.4kW) is actually the core of its claimed advantage — running at roughly half the power while remaining competitive or ahead on throughput is the central efficiency argument OpenAI is making against Nvidia's rack-level power draw assumptions.
insights.quote: Runs normalize to the package TDP, with Jalapeño at 700 watts against the GB200 at 1.2 kilowatts, and the GB300 and MI355X at 1.4 kilowatts.

insights.claim: Jalapeno uses single-token prediction while the Nvidia baselines it is compared against use multi-token prediction (MTP) — a technique using seven tiny draft-model turns plus one batched large-trunk pass to produce up to eight output tokens, reducing expensive large-model passes by up to 8x — meaning Jalapeno's reported advantage is achieved despite using a simpler, less optimized decoding technique than its competition.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is the single most important caveat/strength in the whole comparison: Jalapeno beats Nvidia GB200/GB300 even while running a less favorable decoding algorithm, implying its true advantage over Nvidia hardware would widen further once OpenAI implements multi-token prediction — OpenAI explicitly notes MTP could add another 3-5x latency improvement at iso-efficiency.
insights.quote: Jalapeño uses single-token prediction, whereas the NVIDIA baselines it is compared against use multi-token prediction.

themes.theme: Head-to-head throughput and latency results vs. Nvidia

insights.claim: On GPT-OSS 120B, Jalapeno at 700W shows about 1.9x higher peak mixed tokens-per-second-per-kilowatt and roughly 1.7x lower end-to-end latency versus GB200 at 1,200W at matched operating points, and delivers around 53.7x more throughput than the previous best time-between-tokens.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A ~1.9x throughput-per-watt advantage at lower absolute power is a strong, concrete efficiency data point that — if it holds in broader deployment — supports OpenAI materially reducing its own inference infrastructure power/cost footprint versus continuing to scale on Nvidia GPUs for this workload class.
insights.quote: Jalapeño shows about 1.9x higher peak mixed tokens per second per kilowatt and roughly 1.7x lower end-to-end latency.

insights.claim: On DeepSeek R1 670B (MXFP4), Jalapeno again holds the throughput-per-kW frontier at 700W against GB300 at 1,400W, delivering about 1.7x higher peak mixed tokens/kW and 3.6x lower end-to-end latency, and roughly 104.3x more throughput versus the previous best time-between-tokens.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A larger 670B-parameter MoE model showing an even bigger latency advantage (3.6x) than the smaller GPT-OSS test suggests Jalapeno's architecture scales its efficiency advantage with model size/complexity, which matters most for frontier-scale production inference economics.
insights.quote: Jalapeño delivers about 1.7x higher peak mixed tokens per kilowatt per second and 3.6x lower end-to-end latency, and at the previous best TBT, it offers roughly 104.3x more throughput.

insights.claim: Even in an apples-to-apples test where Jalapeno runs single-token mode directly against GB300 running its native multi-token mode on DeepSeek R1 (removing Jalapeno's speculative-decode advantage entirely), Jalapeno still leads with about 1.5x higher peak mixed-token rate per kilowatt and 2.2x lower end-to-end latency — a narrower but still clearly positive margin.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is the most rigorous, least-favorable-to-OpenAI comparison in the deck, and Jalapeno still wins — this is the strongest evidence that Jalapeno's advantage stems from genuine architectural efficiency rather than just a decoding-technique trick, which should raise investor confidence in the underlying silicon design.
insights.quote: single-token Jalapeño still leads the multi-token GB300, with about 1.5x higher peak mixed-token rate per kilowatt and 2.2x lower end-to-end latency. This margin narrows relative to the plain GB300 comparison but remains clearly positive.

insights.claim: On the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi K2.5 model (MXFP4), Jalapeno at 700W again holds the frontier against GB300 at 1,400W, with about 1.5x higher peak mixed tokens/kW, 3.4x lower end-to-end latency, and roughly 56.1x higher throughput than the previous best time-between-tokens — the largest relative gap shown across all three test models.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Demonstrated performance at trillion-parameter scale (not just smaller models) is direct evidence Jalapeno can serve frontier-class MoE models, which is the exact workload class OpenAI needs for its own largest production models — reinforcing that this isn't a toy benchmark chip.
insights.quote: Kimi K2.5 shows the largest relative gap in the set.

insights.claim: None of the three test models (GPT-OSS, DeepSeek R1, Kimi K2.5) were co-designed for Jalapeno, and OpenAI got all three running on the chip in the window between A0 silicon arriving in the lab and the Hot Chips presentation — i.e., these are out-of-the-box generality results, not hand-tuned showcase numbers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Demonstrating strong results on non-co-designed third-party models addresses a common skepticism about custom ASICs (that they only look good on cherry-picked in-house workloads) — this is a meaningful credibility signal for Jalapeno's general-purpose viability beyond pure OpenAI-model serving.
insights.quote: OpenAI notes none of the three were co-designed for Jalapeño and that it got all of them running between when A0 silicon returned to the lab and now.
insights.locator: Three models to demonstrate generality and velocity

themes.theme: Architecture: one balanced chip vs. heterogeneous fleets

insights.claim: OpenAI's core architectural insight is that a single inference request spans three distinct hardware regimes — compute-bound prefill, a small draft model at ultra-low batch for latency-sensitive speculation, and a memory-bandwidth-bound spec-verify decode with bursty MoE communication — each hitting a different bottleneck, so efficiency only matters if the entire request stays within its end-to-end latency target.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This three-regime framework is a genuinely useful mental model for evaluating any inference chip design — it reframes the challenge away from single-metric FLOPS/bandwidth comparisons toward whole-request latency budgeting, which is the more economically relevant lens for production inference-serving businesses.
insights.quote: a single request spans three hardware stages including a compute-bound prefill, a small draft model at ultra-low batch for latency-sensitive speculation, and a memory-bandwidth-bound spec-verify decode with bursty MoE communication.
insights.locator: A request spans three distinct hardware regimes

insights.claim: OpenAI argues that because workload mixes shift the balance among prefill, draft, and verify phases, specialized/heterogeneous accelerator fleets are inefficient — idle accelerators still draw baseline power — so Jalapeno instead uses a single balanced chip where blocks that idle for a given phase are power-gated, rather than paying for entirely separate accelerators' baseline package/HBM/I/O/network power.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a direct, explicit argument against the increasingly popular industry trend of disaggregated/specialized inference fleets (separate prefill vs. decode hardware); if OpenAI is right, it implies unified balanced-chip designs may out-compete disaggregated fleet architectures on real-world efficiency once idle-power costs are counted — a contrarian bet worth tracking against rivals building disaggregated inference infrastructure.
insights.quote: Workload mixes shift the balance among prefill, draft, and verify, which OpenAI argues makes specialized, heterogeneous fleets inefficient, since idle accelerators still draw baseline power.
insights.locator: Changing ratios → inefficiency in heterogeneous fleets

insights.claim: OpenAI's system design keeps KV cache state local on Jalapeno and varies the active ratio of compute/memory/network per phase (with unused units going dark), rather than moving KV cache across a network between specialized systems at every phase boundary.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Avoiding KV cache network transfer at every phase boundary directly reduces a major latency/bandwidth tax that disaggregated prefill/decode systems must pay — a concrete architectural mechanism explaining Jalapeno's latency advantage, and a design pattern other inference-chip builders may need to match.
insights.quote: OpenAI keeps KV local on Jalapeño and varies the active ratio of compute, memory, and network per phase, with unused units going dark rather than forcing KV to travel across a network at every phase boundary.
insights.locator: System choice: KV moves or the active silicon mix varies

insights.claim: Jalapeno's raw HBM4 bandwidth at 128-chip aggregate scale exceeds one petabyte per second, which on paper implies 1,000-2,000 tokens/second/user without speculative decoding and 5,000-10,000 with it — yet OpenAI acknowledges the real system lands well below either rate, showing that raw bandwidth alone is not the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a rare instance of a chip vendor openly admitting its own theoretical bandwidth ceiling wildly overstates achievable real-world performance — a candid, unusually honest data point that should make investors skeptical of any AI chip vendor's headline 'bandwidth implies X tokens/sec' marketing math across the industry, not just OpenAI's.
insights.quote: a bandwidth-only ceiling implies 1,000 to 2,000 tokens per second per user without speculative decoding and 5,000 to 10,000 with it, yet OpenAI acknowledges the real system lands well below either rate, indicating that raw bandwidth is not the only limiting resource.
insights.locator: Raw HBM bandwidth implies extraordinary token rates

insights.claim: Long-latency memory paths, contended unified memory subsystems, and expensive global memory fences leave compute units waiting on data in transit, reducing utilization — architecture, not raw bandwidth, dominates observed latency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reinforces a general principle applicable across all AI accelerator design: memory system architecture (fences, contention, locality) is frequently the true bottleneck rather than peak bandwidth specs — a useful due-diligence lens for evaluating any vendor's headline bandwidth numbers.
insights.quote: Long-latency paths, contended unified memory subsystems, and expensive global memory fences all leave compute units waiting on data in transit, thereby reducing utilization.

insights.claim: Jalapeno pairs each core slice with an HBM slice for a fast local view and adds a specialized low-latency collective network for common cross-core patterns, while a more flexible general network-on-chip (NoC) handles traffic that doesn't need the fast path — keeping common operands local so data movement doesn't dominate execution.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A dual-network design (specialized fast path plus flexible general path) is the concrete mechanism OpenAI built to solve the memory-locality bottleneck it identified — a specific architectural pattern that could be evaluated against other vendors' interconnect designs (e.g., Google's ICI, Nvidia's NVLink) for relative efficiency.
insights.quote: This architecture responds by pairing each core slice with an HBM slice to provide a fast local view and adding a specialized, low-latency collective network for common cross-core patterns.
insights.locator: Co-design the architecture to address the bottleneck

insights.claim: A local Jalapeno domain reaches 128 ASICs with low core-to-core latency, while a half-flattened two-level Clos topology built around Broadcom Tomahawk6 switches spans a global domain of 2,048 chips, with higher bandwidth allocated for tensor parallel and lower bandwidth for expert parallel traffic.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Confirms Broadcom is a core silicon/systems partner for OpenAI's custom chip program (both the ASIC co-design and the Tomahawk6 switch fabric), meaningfully deepening Broadcom's stake in the custom-AI-silicon supply chain beyond just Google/Meta programs.
insights.quote: a half-flattened two-level Clos topology built around Broadcom Tomahawk6 switches spans a global domain of 2,048 chips, with higher bandwidth for tensor parallel and lower bandwidth for expert parallel.

themes.theme: AI-driven chip design and AI-native programming model

insights.claim: OpenAI used its own internal AI model together with the XLS hardware description language to accelerate chip design, with major changes landing as late as the day of the RTL freeze; the AI-assisted approach measured a 56% PPA (power-performance-area) win on a BF16 multiply unit versus a human baseline, alongside a 10% smaller matrix unit area.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A measured 56% PPA improvement from AI-assisted design over a human engineering baseline is a striking, quantified proof point that AI-driven chip design tools are now delivering meaningfully better results than human designers on specific components — a signal that AI-driven EDA could be a genuine competitive lever for any company (not just OpenAI) racing to design custom silicon faster and better.
insights.quote: It said major changes landed up to the day of the RTL freeze, plus measured PPA wins over a human baseline, such as 56 percent on a BF16 multiply, back-to-back with a 10 percent smaller matrix unit area.
insights.locator: AI helped us build Jalapeño faster and made it better

insights.claim: Jalapeno's programming model is deliberately built to be 'simple for humans and easy for frontier AI to program' — exposing local tensors, fast local paths, and explicit communication so that an AI search system, not a human, can handle the mapping, placement, scheduling, and pipelining that would otherwise be onerous for a person to hand-tune.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a genuinely novel design philosophy: building hardware whose programming model is optimized for AI-driven compilers/optimizers rather than primarily for human programmer ergonomics — a forward-looking bet that could let OpenAI extract far more performance from its own silicon over time as its internal AI optimization tools improve, compounding an advantage competitors using human-centric toolchains may not capture as quickly.
insights.quote: Jalapeño's programming model is built to be simple for humans and easy for frontier AI to program.
insights.locator: Architecture model: Simple for humans to understand

insights.claim: Jalapeno runs a spatial architecture where the Gluon framework programs each physical core as a thread block, with tensor/SIMD/scalar engines organized around a fast local memory view, specialized collectives coordinating cross-core work, and explicit tensor layout information capturing physical placement.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A spatial-architecture programming model is a meaningfully different approach than the CUDA/kernel-launch model dominant on Nvidia GPUs — if it proves more efficient for AI-driven optimization, it could represent a genuine software moat distinct from and complementary to the hardware efficiency gains.
insights.quote: Jalapeño runs a spatial architecture in which the Gluon framework programs each physical core as a thread block.

insights.claim: Starting from functionally correct kernels, an internal OpenAI AI system autonomously drove implementations to high performance, with its optimized attention and MoE kernels running 1.5x to 1.8x faster than existing expert-written implementations, validated end-to-end on-chip.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: AI-optimized kernels beating expert human-written kernels by 1.5-1.8x on validated, on-chip end-to-end runs is a concrete, measurable demonstration that AI-driven kernel optimization is already outperforming top human engineers in production settings — a strong signal for the broader 'AI accelerating AI infrastructure development' recursive-improvement narrative.
insights.quote: Its optimized attention and MoE kernels run 1.5x to 1.8x faster than existing expert-written implementations, validated end-to-end on-chip.
insights.locator: AI turns functional kernels into high-performance implementations

insights.claim: Jalapeno delivers 13.4 PFLOP/s of MXFP4-by-MXFP4 matrix compute, 15.4 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth across 216 GiB, in a 700-watt package, scaling to 27 EFLOP/s and 432 TiB across a full 2,048-chip system, with network bandwidth split at 600 GB/s for the local 128-ASIC domain and 200 GB/s for the global 2,048-ASIC domain.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: These are the hard baseline specs analysts need to directly compare Jalapeno against Nvidia GB200/GB300, Google TPU 8i, Meta MTIA 400, and Microsoft Maia 200 on a normalized FLOPS/watt and bandwidth/watt basis for inference workloads specifically.
insights.quote: Jalapeño delivers 13.4 PFLOP/s of mxfp4 by mxfp4 matrix compute, 15.4 TB/s of HBM4 bandwidth across 216 GiB, and a 700-watt package, scaling to 27 EFLOP/s and 432 TiB across a 2,048-chip system.

insights.claim: OpenAI frames Jalapeno as Gen 1 of a multi-generation roadmap that compounds learnings over time, with Gen 2 targeting better performance-per-watt and Gen 3 aiming for economical, low-latency serving as the architecture unlocks more aggregate HBM bandwidth rather than simply adding more raw bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Explicit multi-generation commitment signals OpenAI intends Jalapeno to be a durable, compounding infrastructure investment (not a one-off experiment) that will keep reducing OpenAI's per-token inference cost over successive generations — a structural long-term negative for how much marginal inference revenue Nvidia can expect to capture from OpenAI specifically.
insights.quote: OpenAI frames Jalapeño as Gen 1 of a multi-generation roadmap that compounds learnings over time. Gen 2 targets better performance per watt, and Gen 3 aims for economical, low-latency serving.

insights.claim: The author's closing take is that Jalapeno is a genuine proof point that AI-assisted chip design (compressed to ~9 months RTL-to-tapeout) can be replicated by other companies, and that the more significant long-term story may be the AI-native software stack itself rather than the chip's raw performance numbers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The author explicitly flags that the broader implication — compressed AI-assisted design cycles becoming a repeatable playbook — matters more than any single chip's benchmark wins, suggesting investors should watch for other well-capitalized AI companies (xAI, Anthropic, Amazon) attempting similarly compressed custom-silicon programs as a copycat trend.
insights.quote: Maybe the more tantalizing bit is how this is a proof point for other companies doing design.
